chapter: Stallings ch 12 — Instruction Sets: Characteristics and Functions (book chapter 12 with Appendix 12A; the syllabus's chapter 10)
note: Drafted 6 Oct 2026 under the instructor's ruling of 5 Oct (questions for 09-18 drafted from the textbook, each approved on /items before students see it). Facts from ch-12.md and the verified draft content/stages/10.draft.md; the Z = (A + B) × C and 0xCAFEF00D examples are the draft's own. Not yet examinable: exams stop at 08.

items.stem: Which four elements does every machine instruction have to specify, explicitly or implicitly?
items.correct: The operation code, source operand references, a result operand reference, and a next instruction reference
distractors: An opcode, a mode field, a condition code, and a register number
A mnemonic, a label, an operand, and a comment
Fetch, decode, execute, and write back
items.rationale: What to do, what to do it to, where to put the result, and where to go next. A mnemonic, label and comment are fields of an assembly-language line, and fetch-decode-execute is the instruction cycle, not the instruction.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — Elements of a Machine Instruction

items.stem: Most instructions carry no explicit reference to the next instruction. Why not?
items.correct: In most cases the next instruction immediately follows the current one, so its address is implicit
distractors: The next instruction is always fetched from the top of the stack
The control unit chooses the next instruction at random from the cache
Each instruction stores its successor's address in the instruction register
items.rationale: Execution is sequential unless an instruction says otherwise, and the program counter already points past the current instruction. Only transfer-of-control instructions need to name the next address.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — 'In most cases, the next instruction to be fetched immediately follows the current instruction.'

items.stem: ADD R, Y means: add the value in data location Y to register R, where Y is a memory address. What is added to R?
items.correct: The value stored at memory location Y
distractors: The address Y itself
The address of register R
The instruction stored at location Y
items.rationale: An operand reference names where a value is; the operation acts on what is there. The book says it plainly: the operation is performed on the contents of a location, not on its address.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — 'Note that the operation is performed on the contents of a location, not on its address.'

items.stem: X and Y are at memory locations 513 and 514. Put the machine instructions for X = X + Y in order.
order: Load a register with the contents of memory location 513
Add the contents of memory location 514 to the register
Store the contents of the register in memory location 513
items.rationale: One high-level statement becomes several machine instructions, each moving data to or from a register. X must be in the register before Y can be added to it, and the sum is only written back once it exists.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — Instruction Types, the X = X + Y example

items.stem: Which four types of instruction must an instruction set provide to express anything a high-level language can?
items.correct: Data processing, data storage, data movement, and control
distractors: Load, store, branch, and halt
Arithmetic, logical, shift, and rotate
Fetch, decode, execute, and interrupt
items.rationale: Data processing is arithmetic and logic; data storage moves data between registers and memory; data movement is I/O; control is test and branch. Shift and rotate are kinds of data processing, and fetch-decode-execute describes the cycle.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — Instruction Types

items.stem: What does a design with fewer addresses per instruction gain, and what does it pay?
items.correct: Shorter, more primitive instructions and a simpler processor, paid for with more instructions per program
distractors: Shorter programs, paid for with a more complex processor
Faster execution of every program, paid for with longer instructions
More registers, paid for with fewer addressing modes
items.rationale: Each address removed makes every instruction shorter and the program longer, which generally means longer execution times. That is why most contemporary machines mix two- and three-address instructions.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — 'Fewer addresses per instruction result in instructions that are more primitive, requiring a less complex processor.'

items.stem: How many instructions does a one-address (accumulator) machine need to compute Z = (A + B) × C?
items.correct: 4: LOAD A, ADD B, MPY C, STOR Z
distractors: 2: ADD and MPY, each naming all three operands
3: MOVE, ADD and MPY
6: PUSH, PUSH, ADD, PUSH, MPY, POP
items.rationale: The accumulator is the implied second operand and the result, so A must be loaded and Z stored explicitly. Two instructions is the three-address version, three the two-address one, and six the zero-address stack machine.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — Number of Addresses (worked with the stage's own example)

items.stem: In a one-address instruction, where are the second operand and the result?
items.correct: In an implied processor register, the accumulator
distractors: On the top of a stack
In the next instruction's address field
In the program counter
items.rationale: One-address machines, common in earlier computers, imply the accumulator: it holds one operand and receives the result. Operands on top of a stack are the zero-address case.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — 'the implied address being a processor register known as the accumulator (AC)'

items.stem: Which are the five fundamental design issues of an instruction set?
items.correct: Operation repertoire, data types, instruction format, registers, and addressing
distractors: Clock rate, cache size, bus width, pipeline depth, and word length
Opcode, operand, mode, register, and condition code
Speed, cost, power, size, and compatibility
items.rationale: These are what an instruction set designer decides: which operations, on what data, in what format, with how many registers, and how operands are addressed. The book adds that they are highly interrelated and must be considered together.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.1 — Instruction Set Design

items.stem: What are the most important general categories of data that machine instructions operate on?
items.correct: Addresses, numbers, characters, and logical data
distractors: Integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and arrays
Bytes, words, doublewords, and quadwords
Registers, immediates, memory, and I/O
items.rationale: Addresses count as data because they are often computed before use. Arrays and strings are high-level structures, bytes and words are sizes rather than kinds, and registers or memory are where operands live, not what they are.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'The most important general categories of data are'

items.stem: How do numbers stored in a computer differ from numbers in ordinary mathematics?
items.correct: Their magnitude is limited and, for floating point, so is their precision
distractors: They can only ever be integers
They have no sign; negative values are simulated in software
They are always stored in decimal
items.rationale: A word has a fixed number of bits, so there is a largest and smallest value, and a floating-point format can only approximate most reals. That is why programmers meet rounding, overflow and underflow.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'First, there is a limit to the magnitude of numbers representable on a machine and second, in the case of floating-point numbers, a limit to their precision.'

items.stem: In machine language, what decides whether the byte 0x37 is the character 7, the number 55, or eight separate flags?
items.correct: The operation that is performed on it
distractors: A type tag stored in memory beside it
The address at which it is stored
The compiler, checking it as the program runs
items.rationale: Bits carry no type. The same data are treated as logical, numerical or text depending on which instruction touches them. Type checking is a high-level-language idea; the compiler is not present when the program runs.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'The “type” of a unit of data is determined by the operation being performed on it.'

items.stem: Among the x86 data types, what is a far pointer?
items.correct: A segment selector together with an offset
distractors: An offset within the current segment
A pointer to a location outside main memory
A 64-bit address used only in long mode
items.rationale: A near pointer is an offset within a segment; a far pointer adds the segment selector, so it can reach a different segment. The distinction comes from the x86's segmented memory.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.3 — Table 12.2, x86 data types

items.stem: Must an x86 doubleword be stored at an address divisible by 4?
items.correct: No: the x86 does not require alignment, though a misaligned item may need more than one bus transfer
distractors: Yes: a misaligned access raises an alignment fault
Yes: the low two address bits are forced to zero
No: the x86 stores every item in bytes, so alignment never matters
items.rationale: The x86 accepts data at any address. The cost appears on the bus, which transfers aligned units, so a misaligned request is split. An alignment fault is one of ARM's optional behaviours, not the x86's.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.3 — x86 Data Types

items.stem: How many bits is a 'word' on ARM, and on the x86?
items.correct: 32 on ARM, 16 on the x86
distractors: 32 on both
16 on ARM, 32 on the x86
64 on both
items.rationale: ARM's sizes are byte, halfword (16) and word (32). The x86 kept the 8086's naming: word (16), doubleword (32), quadword (64). The same word names different sizes, so always check which machine is meant.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.3 — 'ARM processors support data types of 8 (byte), 16 (halfword), and 32 (word) bits in length.'

items.stem: Most ARM processor implementations do not provide floating-point hardware. Why?
items.correct: Leaving it out saves power and area
distractors: ARM cannot represent IEEE 754 numbers
Floating-point work is always sent to an x86 coprocessor
ARM uses packed decimal for all non-integer values
items.rationale: ARM targets small, low-power devices, so hardware many programs never need is left out. Floating point is offered as an optional coprocessor that follows IEEE 754.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.3 — 'The majority of ARM processor implementations do not provide floatingpoint hardware, which saves power and area.'

items.stem: What is the basic idea of the x86's packed SIMD data types?
items.correct: Several operands are packed into one referenced memory item and operated on in parallel
distractors: One operand is split across several registers for extra precision
Data are compressed to save memory and expanded before use
Two instructions are packed into one word and executed together
items.rationale: Single instruction, multiple data: one ADD on a 64-bit packed operand adds, say, eight bytes at once. The packing is of data, not of instructions.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.3 — 'multiple operands are packed into a single referenced memory item and that these multiple operands are operated on in parallel'

items.stem: What is the decimal number 246 in packed decimal?
items.rationale: Each decimal digit gets its own 4-bit code, padded to whole bytes: 0, 2, 4, 6. 1111 0110 is 246 in straight binary; the reversed digits are wrong; and the 0011-prefixed codes are the IRA characters '2', '4', '6'.

items.stem: Packed decimal is less compact than binary. When is it still preferable?
items.correct: When there is a great deal of I/O and comparatively little, simple computation, because it avoids conversion
distractors: When calculations need the highest possible precision
When memory is scarce, because it packs two digits per byte
When numbers must be compared quickly by the ALU
items.rationale: People read and type decimal. Storing decimal digits avoids converting every value on its way in and out, which matters when there is much I/O and little arithmetic. Only 10 of each 16 codes are used, so it costs space.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'it is preferable to store and operate on the numbers in decimal form'

items.stem: Packed decimal marks a negative number with an extra 4-bit sign digit. What is its standard value?
distractors: A 1 in the leftmost bit of the first digit
items.rationale: The standard sign digits are 1100 for + and 1101 for −, placed at either end of the digit string. Neither is a decimal digit (those use 0000 to 1001). A leading 1 bit is the binary sign-bit idea, not packed decimal's.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'Standard sign values are 1100 for positive ( + ) and 1101 for negative ( - ).'

items.stem: How many bits does the IRA (ASCII) code use per character, and how many characters can it represent?
items.correct: 7 bits, so 128 characters
distractors: 8 bits, so 256 characters
16 bits, so 65,536 characters
6 bits, so 64 characters
items.rationale: IRA is a 7-bit code. Characters are almost always stored in 8 bits, but the eighth bit is 0 or a parity bit, not part of the code. 16 bits is a different, larger code altogether.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.2 — 'Each character in this code is represented by a unique 7-bit pattern; thus, 128 different characters can be represented.'

items.stem: Which are the general types of operation found on all machines?
items.correct: Data transfer, arithmetic, logical, conversion, I/O, system control, and transfer of control
distractors: Load, store, add, subtract, branch, call, and return
Fetch, decode, execute, memory access, and write back
Integer, floating point, decimal, and character
items.rationale: The number of opcodes varies widely, but these seven types recur everywhere. Load, add and branch are individual operations within the types; fetch-decode-execute is the cycle; integer and decimal are data types.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.4 — 'the same general types of operations are found on all machines'

items.stem: The character '7' is 0011 0111 in IRA. Which single operation turns it into the number 7 (0000 0111)?
items.correct: AND with 0000 1111
distractors: OR with 0000 1111
XOR with 1111 1111
Logical shift left by 4
items.rationale: AND with a mask keeps the bits where the mask is 1 and clears the rest, so the 0011 prefix goes and the digit stays. OR sets bits, XOR with all 1s inverts every bit, and a shift moves the digit out of place.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.4 — 'the AND operation can be used as a mask that selects certain bits in a word and zeros out the remaining bits'

items.stem: 1100 1000 is −56 in 8-bit two's complement. What does an arithmetic right shift by 2 give?
items.rationale: An arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit into the vacated positions, so it divides by 4 and keeps the sign: −14. 0011 0010 is the logical right shift (0s in), 0010 0011 is a left rotate, and 1110 0100 is a shift by only 1.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.4 — 'On a right arithmetic shift, the sign bit is replicated into the bit position to its right.'

items.stem: What does the processor do to carry out a transfer-of-control instruction?
items.correct: It updates the program counter to the address of some instruction in memory
distractors: It moves the operand from memory into a register
It switches the processor into a privileged mode
It transfers a block of data to an I/O device
items.rationale: Branches, skips and procedure calls all work by changing the PC, so the next instruction fetched is not the one in sequence. Moving operands is data transfer, and entering a privileged state belongs to system control.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.4 — 'the operation performed by the processor is to update the program counter to contain the address of some instruction in memory'

items.stem: Return addresses could be saved in a register or at the start of the procedure. Why is the stack the general answer?
items.correct: It lets procedures nest and allows a procedure to be called again before it has returned
distractors: It is the only memory the processor can write without an address
It is faster than any register
It hides the return address from the procedure being called
items.rationale: A single register or a fixed location holds one return address, so a nested or recursive call overwrites it. A stack keeps one frame per open call, which is exactly what a reentrant procedure needs.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.4 — 'A reentrant procedure is one in which it is possible to have several calls open to it at the same time.'

items.stem: On the x86, how does CMP differ from SUB?
items.correct: Both subtract, but CMP only sets the status flags while SUB also stores the result in the destination
distractors: CMP works only on unsigned numbers, SUB on signed
CMP sets no flags; it only branches
CMP subtracts in the opposite order to SUB
items.rationale: A compare is a subtraction whose result is thrown away; what survives is the flags, which a following conditional jump tests. Whether those flags are read as signed (greater/less) or unsigned (above/below) is the jump's choice.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.5 — 'a compare operation only sets status flags, whereas a subtract operation also stores the result'

items.stem: From the 80286 on, one ENTER instruction replaced the PUSH, MOV, SUB sequence that opens a procedure. How did it compare?
items.correct: It saved space (4 bytes against 6) but took longer to execute (10 clock cycles against 6)
distractors: It was both smaller and faster
It was larger but faster
It was identical in size and speed, only easier to write
items.rationale: A complex instruction can cost more than the simple ones it replaces. Hold on to this: it is the RISC argument of Stage 13 in miniature.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.5 — ENTER 'saves a few bytes of memory compared with the PUSH, MOV, SUB sequence (4 bytes versus 6 bytes), it actually takes longer to execute (10 clock cycles versus 6 clock cycles)'

items.stem: Two unsigned 8-bit pixel values, 200 and 100, are added with MMX saturation arithmetic. What is the result?
items.rationale: With saturation, an overflowing result is set to the largest representable value, 255. Ordinary wraparound addition gives 300 − 256 = 44, which would turn a bright pixel dark. 300 does not fit in 8 bits.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.5 — 'With saturation arithmetic, if addition results in overflow or subtraction results in underflow, the result is set to the largest or smallest value representable.'

items.stem: In the ARM architecture, which instructions may access memory locations?
items.correct: Only load and store instructions; arithmetic and logic work on registers and immediates
distractors: Any instruction, through any addressing mode
Only branch instructions, to fetch their targets
Arithmetic instructions, but only with a memory destination
items.rationale: ARM is a load/store architecture: data are loaded into registers, processed there, and stored back. The x86, by contrast, lets an arithmetic instruction take a memory operand.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.5 — 'only load and store instructions access memory locations; arithmetic and logical instructions are performed only on registers and immediate values encoded in the instruction'

items.stem: What is unusual about how ARM uses condition codes, and what does it cost?
items.correct: Every instruction carries a 4-bit condition field, so almost any instruction can execute conditionally, leaving fewer bits for opcode and operands
distractors: Only branches carry a condition, so other instructions are shorter
Conditions are kept in a separate instruction before each operation
ARM has no condition codes at all
items.rationale: On most machines only branches are conditional. ARM puts the condition in every 32-bit instruction, which removes many branches, at the price of 4 bits in every instruction.
items.source: ch-12.md §12.5 — 'All instructions, not just branch instructions, include a condition code field'

items.stem: The 32-bit value 0xCAFEF00D is stored little endian at address 0x200. Which byte is at address 0x201?
items.correct: 0xF0
distractors: 0xFE
0x0D
0xCA
items.rationale: Little endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address: 0x200 holds 0D, 0x201 holds F0, 0x202 FE, 0x203 CA. 0xFE is what 0x201 holds in big endian.
items.source: ch-12.md §12A — little endian 'stores the least significant byte in the lowest numerical byte address' (the value is the stage's own)

items.stem: What is big endian?
items.correct: Storing the most significant byte of a value at the lowest byte address
distractors: Storing the least significant byte at the lowest byte address
Storing the most significant bit of each byte first
Storing every value on an address divisible by its size
items.rationale: Big endian matches the left-to-right order of Western writing: the big end comes first. The least-significant-byte-first order is little endian, bit order is a separate question, and alignment is unrelated.
items.source: ch-12.md §12A — 'stores the most significant byte in the lowest numerical byte address; this is known as big endian'

items.stem: The character string "CPE" is stored in memory on a big-endian machine and on a little-endian machine. How do the two byte orders compare?
items.correct: They are the same: each character is its own one-byte item, and endianness only orders bytes within one item
distractors: They are reversed: "EPC" on the little-endian machine
They differ in every second byte
They are the same only if the string's length is a multiple of 4
items.rationale: Endianness reverses the bytes inside one multibyte value; it never reorders separate items. A string is an array of one-byte characters, so both machines store it the same way.
items.source: ch-12.md §12A — 'The property of endianness does not extend beyond an individual data unit.'

items.stem: Which of these machines is little endian?
items.correct: The Intel x86
distractors: The IBM System/370
The Motorola 680x0
The Sun SPARC
items.rationale: The x86, VAX and Alpha are little endian; the IBM System 370/390, the Motorola 680x0, Sun SPARC and most RISC machines are big endian.
items.source: ch-12.md §12A — 'Some machines, such as the Intel 80x86, x86, VAX, and Alpha, are little-endian machines'

items.stem: What is a bi-endian processor, and what does it allow?
items.correct: One that supports both big- and little-endian modes, so software moved from another machine can keep its byte order
distractors: One that stores the high half of a word big endian and the low half little endian
One that converts every value between orders on each memory access
One that has no byte order because it addresses only whole words
items.rationale: The PowerPC supports both modes, and developers choose one when migrating operating systems and applications. ARM's E-bit, set by SETEND, is the same idea under program control.
items.source: ch-12.md §12A — 'The PowerPC is a bi-endian processor that supports both big-endian and littleendian modes.'
